query_text: Propose an image or an event that defines the twentieth century.

parts.text:
To capture the essence of the twentieth century in a single image, one must look for a visual that synthesizes its greatest contradictions: its unparalleled technological leaps, its devastating geopolitical rivalries, and its profound shifts in how humanity viewed itself. 

The image that defines the twentieth century is **"Earthrise,"** photographed by astronaut William Anders during the Apollo 8 mission on **December 24, 1968**. 

At first glance, it is a photograph of space. But in reality, it is the most important portrait of Earth ever taken. 

Here is why this single image defines the twentieth century:

---

### 1. The Backdrop of a Fractured Century
To understand the power of "Earthrise," one must look at the year it was taken: 1968. It was perhaps the most turbulent year of a highly fractured century. The world was tearing itself apart: the Vietnam War was raging, the Soviet Union had just invaded Czechoslovakia to crush the Prague Spring, and the United States was reeling from the assassinations of Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert F. Kennedy, alongside widespread civil rights protests. 

The twentieth century was defined by ideological warfare—Fascism, Communism, and Democratic Capitalism clashing in conflicts that cost tens of millions of lives. Yet, at the height of this global discord, three human beings slipped gravity’s pull and looked back. 

### 2. The Triumph of Technological Acceleration
The twentieth century saw a rate of technological progress unlike any other period in human history. Humanity went from the Wright brothers' first tentative 12-second flight in 1903 to putting a man on the moon in 1969. 

"Earthrise" is the ultimate monument to this acceleration. The technology required to take this photo—computing power, rocketry, materials science—was the pinnacle of industrial-age ingenuity. Yet, in a supreme historical irony, this technology was birthed by the Cold War. The Saturn V rocket that propelled Apollo 8 was a direct descendant of the V-2 missiles of World War II and the Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles (ICBMs) designed to carry nuclear warheads. "Earthrise" captures this dual nature of 20th-century technology: weapons of absolute destruction repurposed for absolute wonder.

### 3. The Death of Borders
For millennia, human history was defined by maps, borders, empires, and territory. The conflicts of the twentieth century were fought over lines drawn on dirt. 

But in "Earthrise," those lines vanish. The photograph shows a swirling, vibrant marble of blue, white, and brown, suspended in an unforgiving, velvety black void. From that distance, there is no West versus East, no capitalism versus communism, no rich versus poor. There is only a single, fragile ecosystem. As poet Archibald MacLeish wrote of the image at the time, it forced humanity to see themselves as "riders on the earth together, brothers on that bright loveliness in the eternal cold."

### 4. The Birth of Global Consciousness
The twentieth century was the century of mass industrialization, atomic energy, and unprecedented exploitation of natural resources. By the 1960s, the ecological consequences of this progress were beginning to surface. 

"Earthrise" acted as a psychological mirror. By showing the Earth as a finite, delicate oasis in an infinite desert, it catalyzed the modern environmental movement. Within two years of the photo being published, the first Earth Day was celebrated (1970), and organizations like Greenpeace and Doctors Without Borders were born. It forced humanity to realize that the "progress" of the 20th century came with a heavy cost, and that our home had limits.

---

### Conclusion
As William Anders famously reflected: **"We came all this way to explore the Moon, and the most important thing is that we discovered the Earth."**

The twentieth century was an age of extremes—of immense violence and staggering progress, of terrifying division and grand ambition. "Earthrise" captures all of this. It is an image born of a military-industrial space race, yet it delivered a message of peace. It is the definitive image of the twentieth century because it marked the exact moment humanity finally stepped outside of its cradle, looked back, and realized just how precious, and how lonely, we really are.
